slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 0: Before you begin. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 0, treat About this expanded volume as a design decision with costs and evidence. Modern C++ Programming Resource Safety, Generic Programming, the Standard Library, and Modern Language Design C++ From Beginner to Expert · Book II Dr. Charles Dorner · Expanded manuscript · 2026 A program can compile, print the expected answer, and still leave its next caller with a dangling reference. A resource wrapper can release memory correctly while a failed update publishes half of a new dataset. A view can make a transformation elegant while hiding that its input has already disappeared. Modern C++ is not a collection of newer syntax that makes these problems vanish. It is a way to make ownership, values, constraints, and state transitions explicit enough to reason about them. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

Begin after you can write functions, use basic containers, understand references and pointers, define simple classes, and compile a multi-file application. Book I supplies that foundation. This volume revisits lifetime and class invariants when modern features make those ideas more demanding; it does not assume that a short introduction to pointers already resolves every ownership question. Chapters 1–6 establish values, invariants, RAII, copying, moving, and smart ownership. Chapters 7–10 develop meaningful operators, inheritance, runtime polymorphism, and composition. Chapters 11–18 cover templates, concepts, lambdas, iterators, containers, algorithms, and ranges. Chapters 19–21 integrate richer result types, external resources, and a complete reporting application. The appendices provide complete supplemental programs and a reusable review method. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

CMake requests that mode explicitly and disables compiler-specific language extensions for the examples. The reference directory retains links to the C++20 working draft N4861 and relevant original project documentation. It also identifies living primary documents used for editorial cross-checks. A living draft can contain features or wording newer than C++20; it is not silently treated as the deployed language baseline. The examples avoid relying on later conveniences such as C++23 range-to-container helpers or optional monadic operations. Each chapter begins with a concrete problem, develops the numbered concepts, and walks through complete source from the companion. The guided lab then changes one requirement or introduces one failure boundary. Read the explanations between listings. They identify owners, starting state, permitted inputs, and the difference between a local observation and a general guarantee.
